subject: polis

brief.inclusion: Internet entrepreneur turned Democratic governor of Colorado (2019–January 2027) who used his own fortune to remake Colorado politics, first as one of the 2004 "Gang of Four" donors and then as a record self-funding candidate, and who breaks with his party on libertarian grounds.

summary: Co-founder of bluemountain.com and ProFlowers who became one of Colorado's biggest political funders, helping finance the 2004 "Gang of Four" network that flipped the legislature, then spending a state-record $18 million or more of his own money to win the governorship in 2018. Colorado's first Jewish governor and the first openly gay man elected governor of any state, he chaired the National Governors Association in 2024–25 and leaves office in January 2027 after his own party censured him in May 2026 for commuting the sentence of election denier Tina Peters.

chapters.title: An internet fortune
chapters.dek: E-cards, flowers and two sales worth over a billion dollars.
chapters.body:
Polis was born Jared Schutz in Boulder on May 12, 1975, the son of Stephen Schutz and Susan Polis Schutz, founders of the greeting-card publisher Blue Mountain Arts [[wikipedia]]. He graduated from Princeton in 1996 and that year co-founded bluemountain.com, a free electronic-card site. In 1999 it was sold to Excite@Home for $430 million in stock and $350 million in cash [[wikipedia]].

He founded the online florist ProFlowers in 1998; renamed Provide Commerce, it went public in 2003 and was bought by Liberty Media in 2005 for $477 million. In 2006 he co-founded the Boulder accelerator Techstars [[wikipedia]]. In 2000 he legally took his mother's maiden name, Polis [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Turning money into political power
chapters.dek: The Gang of Four, a 90-vote school-board race and a seat in Congress.
chapters.body:
Polis entered politics in 2000, winning an at-large seat on the Colorado State Board of Education by 90 votes [[wikipedia]]. In 2004 he was one of four wealthy Colorado Democrats, later called the "Gang of Four," who funded a network of outside groups that helped Democrats take both chambers of the legislature [[copo-2018]].

In 2008 he won the open 2nd congressional district with 63 percent after spending a then-record $6 million of his own money in the primary, becoming the first openly gay man elected to Congress as a non-incumbent [[wikipedia, copo-2018]]. In 2014 he financed ballot measures to restrict oil and gas drilling, then withdrew them in a deal with Gov. John Hickenlooper [[wikipedia, copo-2018]].

chapters.title: Governor
chapters.dek: A record self-funded campaign and two terms.
chapters.body:
Polis ran for governor in 2018 on universal preschool and kindergarten, 100 percent renewable electricity by 2040 and reducing inequality, and spent more than $18 million of his own money, a state record [[jta-2018, copo-2018]]. He beat Republican Walker Stapleton with 53.4 percent, becoming Colorado's first Jewish governor and the first openly gay man elected governor in the U.S. [[jta-2018, wikipedia]]. "I derive a lot of the values that I try to bring into the public sphere from my private faith," he said [[jta-2018]].

In office he signed a red-flag gun law and a ban on conversion therapy for minors in 2019, pardoned 1,351 people for marijuana possession in 2021, and in 2023 signed laws raising the gun-purchase age to 21 and protecting abortion and gender-affirming care [[wikipedia]]. He was reelected in 2022 with 58.5 percent and chaired the National Governors Association from July 2024 to July 2025 [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: A libertarian Democrat at odds with his party
chapters.dek: RFK Jr., vetoes and the Tina Peters commutation.
chapters.body:
Polis often breaks with his party on libertarian grounds. In November 2024 he wrote that he was "excited" by Trump's choice of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to run the Health and Human Services Department, praising Kennedy's help against vaccine mandates in Colorado in 2019 and hoping he would favor "personal choice on vaccines rather than bans." After an outcry, he added that "science must remain THE cornerstone" of health policy, and his office said he still opposed Kennedy's positions on vaccines and fluoride [[cbs-rfk-2024]]. In 2025 he vetoed several Democratic bills, and the legislature overrode him on a social-media bill [[wikipedia]].

The sharpest break came over Tina Peters, the former Mesa County clerk serving nine years for a breach of election equipment tied to false claims about the 2020 election. Trump had attacked Polis for not freeing her and issued a symbolic federal pardon. In May 2026 Polis commuted her sentence to 4.5 years, calling it "extremely unusual and lengthy" for a first-time nonviolent offender, and she was paroled June 1 [[ap-censure-2026, tnd-censure-2026]]. On May 20 about 90 percent of the Colorado Democratic Party's roughly 700-member central committee voted to censure him, barring him from appearing as a featured guest at party events [[ap-censure-2026, tnd-censure-2026]]. Term-limited, he leaves office in January 2027 [[tnd-censure-2026]]. That October he was managing flood emergencies across 12 southwestern counties [[colorado-sun-flood-2026]].
